title: Study types: what each can and can't show
goal: Name the main study designs, from mechanistic work to meta-analyses and consensus statements, and say which questions each can and can't answer.

steps.title: Watch or intervene: two families of studies
steps.text:
Every study either **watches** or **intervenes** [[c:exp-vs-obs]].

- In an **observational** study the researchers only measure: who trains how, who gets injured, who is fast. They assign nothing.
- In an **experimental** study they decide who gets what: caffeine or placebo, training block A or block B.

A third kind sits beside these: the [mechanistic study](g:mechanistic-study). It looks inside the body (cells, enzymes, muscle biopsies, animals) to show *how* something could work, for example which enzymes rise after interval training.

Each answers a different question. Watching shows what goes together; intervening tests what causes what; mechanism explains how. Many mistakes in reading science come from asking a study a question its design can't answer.

claims.text: Studies are experimental or observational, depending on whether the investigator assigns the exposure.

evidence.quote: Clinical research falls into two general categories: experimental and observational, based on whether the investigator assigns the exposures or not.

steps.title: Snapshots and follow-ups
steps.text:
Two observational designs matter most [[c:obs-designs]]:

| design | what it does | example |
|---|---|---|
| [cross-sectional](g:cross-sectional-study) | measures everything once: a snapshot | VO2max and weekly hours in 300 club cyclists, in one week |
| [cohort](g:cohort-study) | follows people forward in time | 500 marathoners tracked for injuries for a year |

Both can show an **association**: two things that go together. Neither can prove cause, because of [confounders](g:confounder): third factors linked to both. Cyclists who ride more hours have a higher VO2max, but talented riders also tend to ride more.

A cohort beats a snapshot because it shows what came first. The confounders remain.

claims.text: Cohort studies follow people forward from exposure to outcome; cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time point.

evidence.quote: Within analytical studies, cohort studies track people forward in time from exposure to outcome.
Cross-sectional studies are like a snapshot, which measures both exposure and outcome at one time point.

steps.title: Randomised trials and crossovers
steps.text:
In a [randomised controlled trial](g:rct) (RCT), chance decides who gets the treatment. With enough people, randomisation balances the groups on everything, including factors nobody measured, so a difference at the end can be put down to the treatment. A placebo and blinding stop expectations from doing the work.

In a **parallel** RCT each person gets one condition. In a [crossover](g:crossover-study) each athlete does every condition, in random order, with a washout between. Each athlete is their own control, so far fewer are needed [[c:crossover-n]].

Crossovers suit effects that wear off: caffeine before a time trial, yes; 12 weeks of training, no, because fitness carries over into the next condition.

claims.text: A crossover design needs far fewer athletes than a fully controlled parallel trial to detect the same small performance effect.

evidence.quote: Using change in performance in events as the outcome measure in a crossover study, researchers could delimit such enhancements with a sample of 16-65 athletes, or with 65-260 in a fully controlled study.

steps.title: Reviews, meta-analyses and consensus
steps.text:
One study is rarely enough, so some studies pull many others together:

- A [systematic review](g:systematic-review) searches for *every* study on a question, with rules fixed in advance, and judges the quality of each.
- A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) goes one step further and pools their results into one effect estimate [[c:sr-ma]].
- A [consensus statement](g:consensus-statement) is a panel of experts (IOC, ACSM, ISSN) reading the evidence and writing recommendations. It mixes evidence with expert judgement, which helps where trials are missing.

A systematic review is not the same as an ordinary (narrative) review. In a narrative review the author chooses which studies to discuss, so it can cherry-pick.

claims.text: A systematic review selects the studies; a meta-analysis statistically pools them into a single effect size.

evidence.quote: The systematic review (the process of selecting the studies) and meta-analysis (the statistical aggregation that produces a single effect size) are tools to consume and apply the evidence by stakeholders.

steps.title: Match the question to the design
steps.text:
Each design answers some questions and not others:

| design | can show | can't show |
|---|---|---|
| mechanistic | how an effect could work | that performance changes |
| cross-sectional | what goes together now | what came first, or cause |
| cohort | what comes before what | cause, because of confounders |
| RCT or crossover | cause, in people like those studied | effects in very different people |
| systematic review, meta-analysis | the overall picture | more than its studies allow |

Before trusting a headline ("coffee drinkers run faster"), ask which design it came from and whether that design can answer the claim being made.

points: Observational studies only measure; experiments assign the exposure; mechanistic studies show how something could work.
Cross-sectional studies are snapshots and cohorts follow people forward: both show association, not cause, because of confounders.
Randomisation balances groups on measured and unmeasured factors; a crossover makes each athlete their own control and needs far fewer people.
Crossovers fit short-acting treatments (caffeine, bicarbonate), not training blocks that carry over.
A systematic review finds and appraises every study; a meta-analysis pools them; a consensus statement adds expert judgement.

variants.stem: Researchers record VO2max and usual weekly riding hours in 300 club cyclists, all in the same week. What design is this?

options.text: Cross-sectional study
options.why: Right: everything is measured once, at one time point: a snapshot.

options.text: Cohort study
options.why: A cohort follows people forward in time; here nobody is followed up.

options.text: Parallel-group RCT
options.why: Nobody is assigned to a treatment, so it isn't an experiment.

options.text: Crossover study
options.why: Nobody does two conditions; the researchers only measure.

variants.stem: At the start of a season, 400 marathon runners report their weekly strength training. Researchers then record their injuries for 12 months. What design is this?

options.text: Cross-sectional study
options.why: A snapshot would measure training and injuries at the same moment; here runners are followed for a year.

options.text: Cohort study
options.why: Right: people are tracked forward in time from exposure (strength training) to outcome (injury).

options.text: Parallel-group RCT
options.why: The runners chose their own training; nobody was randomised to it.

options.text: Crossover study
options.why: Each runner lives one season with their own habits; nobody does both conditions.

variants.stem: Twenty triathletes each do a 40 km bike time trial twice, once after caffeine and once after placebo, in random order a week apart. What design is this?

options.text: Cross-sectional study
options.why: This is an experiment: the researchers assign caffeine and placebo.

options.text: Cohort study
options.why: Nobody is simply followed over time; the researchers assign the conditions.

options.text: Parallel-group RCT
options.why: In a parallel RCT each athlete would get only one condition; here each gets both.

options.text: Crossover study
options.why: Right: every athlete does both conditions in random order, so each is their own control.

variants.stem: What makes a study experimental rather than observational?

options.text: The researchers decide who gets the exposure
options.why: Right: experiments assign the exposure; observational studies only measure what people already do.

options.text: It takes place in a laboratory
options.why: Lab studies can be observational (testing runners once) and experiments can run in the field.

options.text: It measures a large number of people
options.why: Size doesn't define the design: a cohort can have 100,000 people and an experiment 10.

options.text: It compares a group with a control group
options.why: Analytical observational studies, such as cohorts, also have comparison groups.

variants.stem: Researchers take thigh muscle biopsies from 12 cyclists before and after 6 weeks of interval training and find a key mitochondrial enzyme up by 30%. What does this study show?

options.text: How the muscle changed, not that race performance improved
options.why: Right: it is mechanistic work: it shows a change inside the muscle, but performance was never measured.

options.text: That interval training makes cyclists faster in races
options.why: No race or time trial was measured; a rise in an enzyme is a step on the way, not the result.

options.text: That intervals beat steady riding for fitness
options.why: There was no steady-riding group to compare with.

options.text: Nothing, because biopsies can't be trusted
options.why: Biopsies are a standard, useful tool; the limit is what the study measured, not the method.

variants.stem: A cross-sectional study of 300 club cyclists finds that those who ride more hours per week have higher VO2max. Can we conclude that riding more raises VO2max?

options.text: No: a snapshot can't show what came first, and talent may drive both
options.why: Right: high-VO2max riders may simply enjoy riding more. A snapshot shows association only.

options.text: Yes: with 300 riders the sample is large enough
options.why: A larger sample makes the association more precise, not causal. Confounding doesn't shrink with n.

options.text: Yes, as long as the result has p < 0.05
options.why: A small p-value only says the data would be surprising if there were no association; it can't tell cause from confounding.

options.text: No: observational studies are always wrong
options.why: Observational studies are often right about associations; they just can't prove cause on their own.

variants.stem: In a cohort of 400 runners, those who did strength training had fewer injuries over a year. Which is the most likely confounder?

options.text: Experience: veterans lift more and get injured less
options.why: Right: experience is linked to both the exposure (strength training) and the outcome (injury), so it can create the association by itself.

options.text: Strength training itself, the exposure studied
options.why: That is the exposure being studied, not a third factor.

options.text: The injuries recorded over the year
options.why: That is the outcome, not a third factor.

options.text: The number of runners followed in the cohort
options.why: Sample size affects precision, not confounding.

variants.stem: Why do trials let chance decide who gets the treatment?

options.text: To balance the groups on everything, measured or not
options.why: Right: with enough people, randomisation spreads confounders (talent, sleep, diet) evenly, so a difference can be put down to the treatment.

options.text: To make the groups larger
options.why: Randomisation doesn't change the number of people; it changes how they are split.

options.text: To stop athletes from knowing what they got
options.why: That is blinding, often used with a placebo; randomisation is a separate step.

options.text: To make the results apply to all athletes
options.why: Results apply to people like those studied; randomisation protects against bias, not narrow samples.

variants.stem: Which cycling question would a crossover study answer best?

options.text: Does caffeine improve 40 km time-trial power?
options.why: Right: caffeine wears off within a day, so each rider can do both conditions with a short washout.

options.text: Does 12 weeks of polarised training raise VO2max more than threshold training?
options.why: Fitness from the first block carries over into the second, which spoils a crossover unless the washout is months long.

options.text: Do cyclists who ride more get more knee pain over 5 years?
options.why: This is about habits people choose over years: a cohort question, not an experiment.

options.text: Does a year of strength training improve cycling economy?
options.why: A year-long training effect would carry over into the next condition.

variants.stem: Which running question would a crossover study answer best?

options.text: Does sodium bicarbonate before a 1,500 m race improve time?
options.why: Right: the effect lasts hours, so each runner can try both conditions a few days apart.

options.text: Does a 16-week marathon plan beat a 12-week plan?
options.why: Training effects carry over from one condition to the next, so a parallel RCT fits better.

options.text: Do runners who stretch get fewer injuries over 2 years?
options.why: This asks about chosen habits over years: a cohort question.

options.text: Does a year of strength training improve running economy?
options.why: Strength gained in the first condition would still be there during the second.

variants.stem: Why does a crossover study usually need far fewer athletes than a parallel RCT?

options.text: Each athlete is their own control, so differences between athletes drop out
options.why: Right: comparing each athlete with themselves removes the big between-athlete spread from the comparison.

options.text: Crossover studies don't need a placebo
options.why: Crossovers often use a placebo; that isn't why they need fewer people.

options.text: Each athlete is tested twice, which doubles the sample size
options.why: Two tests on the same person aren't two people; the gain comes from within-athlete comparison.

options.text: Crossover studies only include well-trained athletes
options.why: Any population can be studied in a crossover; the design, not the sample, saves numbers.

variants.stem: What does a meta-analysis add to a systematic review?

options.text: It pools the studies' results into one effect estimate
options.why: Right: the systematic review finds and appraises the studies; the meta-analysis combines their numbers.

options.text: It runs a new, larger trial
options.why: A meta-analysis uses existing studies; it collects no new data.

options.text: It picks the best study and reports only that
options.why: It combines all suitable studies rather than choosing one.

options.text: It adds expert opinion on what athletes should do
options.why: That describes a consensus statement.

variants.stem: An IOC consensus statement on sports nutrition is best described as:

options.text: An expert panel's recommendations after reviewing the evidence
options.why: Right: it combines the evidence with expert judgement, useful where trials are missing.

options.text: The largest randomised trial on the topic
options.why: A consensus statement runs no trial of its own.

options.text: A statistical pooling of all trials on the topic
options.why: That is a meta-analysis; a consensus statement may use one, but adds judgement.

options.text: A survey of what elite athletes actually do
options.why: Common practice isn't evidence that it works.
